title: Next-Word Machines
about: How a chatbot builds an answer one likely word at a time.

cards.prompt: As you type, your phone suggests the next word. A chatbot does the same thing on a much bigger scale: it has read a huge amount of text, and guesses what usually comes next. Which word is it **most likely** to pick here?
cards.context: I'm so hungry, I could eat a
cards.hint: What does the chatbot learn from: what's sensible to eat, or what people often write? Think of a saying people often write.
cards.nudge: That's a sensible thing to eat, but the chatbot isn't choosing food. Which ending have you heard people say most often?
cards.explanation: "I could eat a **horse**" is a common saying, so it turns up in text far more often than any sensible snack. The model picks what usually comes next, not what makes sense, or what's true.

cards.title: Guessing the next word
cards.body: A chatbot is built on a **language model**. It has read a huge amount of text, so it knows which words usually come next. It reads all the text so far, then gives each possible next word a **chance**: after "The cat sat on the", "mat" 60%, "sofa" 20%, "moon" 5%. It picks one, adds it, and repeats.

cards.prompt: Put the steps a chatbot repeats for every word in order. Once a word is added, it stays: the model never goes back to change it.

items.label: Read all the text so far
Give each possible next word a chance
Add it to the end of the text

cards.hint: It can't pick a word before it knows the chances, and it can't work out the chances before it has read the text.
cards.nudge: Start with what the model needs first: the text so far. What does it need before it can pick?
cards.explanation: **Read** the text so far, give each next word a **chance**, **pick** one, **add** it. Then the loop starts again with the longer text. (Really it works with word-pieces, but words are close enough.)

cards.prompt: After "The cat sat on the", "mat" had the biggest chance. Now the text is different, with more before it. Which word is **most likely** next this time?
cards.context: Strapped in for launch, the cat sat in its
cards.hint: Step one of the loop is to read **all** the text so far. Which words at the start change the picture?
cards.nudge: The model reads everything, including "Strapped in for launch". What do you get strapped into on a rocket?
cards.explanation: The model reads **all** the text so far, so "Strapped in for launch" changes the chances: **seat** goes to the top and "mat" drops. Different words earlier in the text can lead to a different next word.

cards.prompt: After "The cat sat on the", the model happens to pick the unlikely word "moon". What happens next?

options.text: "moon" is now part of the text, so it works out the next word from there
It spots that "moon" was unlikely, goes back and swaps it for "mat"
options.nudge: Look at the loop again: read, chance, pick, add. Is there a step that goes back and changes a word?

options.text: It ignores "moon" and works out the next word from "The cat sat on the"
options.nudge: Step one is to read **all** the text so far. What's in the text now?

options.text: It stops writing, because an unlikely word means the answer has gone wrong
options.nudge: The model doesn't judge its own picks. It just keeps going round the loop.

cards.hint: Follow the loop one more time. After a word is picked and added, what does the model read next?
cards.explanation: The loop never goes back. "moon" is added, so the next chances are worked out from "The cat sat on the moon", and the rest of the answer follows on from it. One odd pick can steer everything after it.

cards.prompt: After "Fish and", a model gives "chips" a **70%** chance. That means it picks "chips" about 70 times in every 100, not every time. If it carries on from "Fish and" **10** times, about how many times will it pick "chips"?
cards.hint: 70 out of every 100 is the same share as how many out of every 10?
cards.nudge: A chance isn't "always". 70 in 100 is the same share as 7 in 10.
cards.explanation: About **7** times out of 10. A chance is "how often", not "always": the other 3 times it picks something else, like "peas".

cards.prompt: A chatbot writes "The Eiffel Tower is in Paris". How did it come up with that?

options.text: It looked it up on a map before it answered
options.nudge: A language model on its own doesn't look things up. What did it learn from?

options.text: It understands where famous places are, like a person
options.nudge: It doesn't understand places. Think about how it chooses each word.

options.text: It checked the fact was true before writing it
options.nudge: It doesn't check facts as it writes. Each word is a guess about what usually comes next.

options.text: Those words often appear together in the text it learned from

cards.hint: Think back to how it picks every word.
cards.explanation: "Eiffel Tower" and "Paris" appear together in a huge amount of text, so "Paris" gets a high chance. It's right because the pattern was common, not because it checked. Real chatbots get extra training so their likely words make helpful answers, and some apps can search the web, but the words are still written this way.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- A **language model** gives each possible next word a chance.
- It picks one, adds it, and repeats until it's done.
- Likely isn't the same as checked or true.

Next: the setting that decides how adventurous its picks are.
